When shopping for chinos or any other type of pants, the fabric choice is crucial, as it impacts comfort, durability, and overall appearance. Typically, chinos are made with a lightweight cotton blend to create a more comfortable wear for men. While many modern chinos incorporate stretch or performance fibers, traditional 100% cotton options are still widely available. Here’s a rundown of common fabrics and what they’re best for:.

Sources indicate that A classic choice for chinos due to its softness, breathability, and comfort. Cotton is ideal for casual wear and everyday use. It can be found in various weights and finishes, from lightweight and airy to heavier and more structured.

Recent findings suggest that this is a type of weave rather than a fabric itself. Twill fabrics, often made from cotton, have a diagonal pattern that adds durability and a subtle texture.

Often used in blends, polyester adds durability and wrinkle resistance. It’s less breathable than cotton but can help chinos maintain their shape and resist stains. Polyester blends are ideal for a polished look with low maintenance.

Industry observers note that many chinos use fabric blends to combine the best properties of different materials. Common blends include cotton-polyester (for durability and wrinkle resistance) or cotton-spandex (for stretch and flexibility). Blends can provide a good balance of comfort, durability, and ease of care.

According to recent reports, fabrics with added spandex or elastane offer flexibility and comfort. These are great for chinos that need to accommodate a range of movements and provide a snug fit without losing their shape.

Chinos should fit comfortably around your waist and hips without being too tight or too loose. Look for options with a bit of stretch, as they often offer a better fit and more flexibility. When searching for the best chinos, you'll typically come across these main fits below.

A modern, tailored look that tapers slightly from the thigh down. The leg should taper slightly but not be so slim that it looks like skinny jeans. Great for guys who prefer a more streamlined silhouette without being too tight.

A classic, timeless cut that falls straight from the hips to the ankles. This fit works well for most body types and offers a more relaxed yet polished look.

Industry observers note that designed for guys with more muscular thighs, this fit offers extra room in the seat and thighs while still tapering toward the ankle. It gives a tailored look without feeling restrictive.

A roomier option with more space in the thigh and leg, ideal for casual wear or those who prioritize comfort over a tapered leg.

To find the best chinos, our fashion team, led by Style Director Christian Gollayan, focused on these key factors: style, fit, comfort, price point, versatility, and performance (including stretch, moisture-wicking, and breathability). We examined whether they fit true to size, whether the fabric could withstand hours of movement in different temperatures, and whether they could be worn for more than one occasion.

It has been revealed that our tested selection doesn't chase trends, rather it highlights chinos for men that fit great (even on athletic guys with bigger thighs), provide strong value and performance, and come in styles that'll still look sharp years from now. Keep reading to find out which pairs earned their stripes and landed a spot on our handpicked list.

Sources indicate that when it comes to styling chinos for men, it's essential to strike the perfect balance between looking casual and looking polished. For starters, the safest way to style chinos is to opt for versatile colors like classic khaki, navy, or olive. Then, ensure your chinos have the right fit—a tailored fit, preferably, that accentuates your silhouette and is not too loose or tight. Then, for a smart-casual vibe, pair your chinos with crisp button-down shirts or polo shirts for your office days. For something a bit more laidback, dress down your chinos with a well-fitted t-shirt or sweater for your casual outings. For layering, chinos will match well with blazers and shackets for colder seasons. As for footwear, canvas sneakers and loafers in general will give your chinos a more casual feel, while leather sneakers and dress shoes are perfect for dressing up chinos for a more put-together look. We also encourage wearing chinos with a leather belt.

It has been revealed that if you're a fit guy looking for chinos that'll match your athletic build, we have some recommendations. Typically, guys who have larger legs will find that off-the-rack chinos are loose around the waist. Bodybuilders tend to run into this problem where they have to size up to get normal chinos to fit their quads, but since they have a slighter waist, it’s often loose. For maximum comfort, look for pants with more room in the quads and glutes while tapering up the waist for an athletic fit.

In a recent development, in short, chinos are a style of trousers, whereas khaki mainly refers to a light brown or tan color. Specifically, chinos are pants typically made of cotton twill fabric, which is durable, light, and breathable, and come in a variety of colors beyond the traditional khaki. Khakis often mean pants made in khaki colors and the term is now often used to describe casual cotton trousers often in a beige or tan color.

While khakis share similarities with chinos, the term is sometimes used more narrowly to refer specifically to beige or tan-colored casual pants, whereas chinos specifically refer to a pants style made in a certain fabric and design.

So all khakis can be chinos, but not all chinos are necessarily khakis since chinos can come in every color imaginable.

Sources indicate that modern chinos are often made with cotton blends that incorporate a little stretch for added flexibility and comfort. Performance-oriented versions may also use fabrics like polyester or nylon to add features such as moisture-wicking, breathability, or quick-drying properties. Traditional 100% cotton chinos are still widely available, too.

You bet your ass we do! Chinos remain a wardrobe staple in men's fashion because they’re so versatile, comfortable, and stylish for different occasions. They can be dressed up or down for a casual day out, a semi-formal event, or even an office day in the workplace. Since chinos are often made of soft, breathable, and light fabric, they can transition from warm summers to cooler days. Men’s chinos are also popular because they are super easy to style—whether it’s for your workplace attire or your weekend wear, they will find a way to be part of your fit. Lastly, chino pants just have that classic, clean, enduring appeal, making them the go-to pants style for many men.

Latest Update: FDA Initiates Labeling Changes for GLP-1s Due to Rare But Serious Eye Disease Risk

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 people have a latest symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.
  • Industry observers note that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S.
  • A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GLP-1 people have a latest symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

Industry observers note that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) unveiled on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint noted.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

The study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

According to recent reports, in a 2024 podcast, Rizzo remarked he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

About 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:.

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:.

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 users “challenging” to interpret.

It has been revealed that across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint stated patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:.

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint said that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:.

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the newly introduced warning on the drugs’ labels.

In a recent development, amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the tech giant is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The upcoming Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

In a recent development, both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a new Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

According to recent reports, the bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

According to recent reports, the higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

As much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

Recent findings suggest that the Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

In a recent development, those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

If you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ford may be talking up the fresh Fathom EV as its latest “Model T moment,” but the Blue Oval arguably already had one this century, and it’s called the Maverick. The compact unibody pickup landed in 2021 with a splash worthy of Homer Simpson off a high dive, thanks to its mix of truck bed utility, car-like ride and handling, and available hybrid power, all—technically if not practically—available for under $20,000.

Prices have admittedly climbed since then, even outpacing inflation, and the lineup has seen its fair share of rejiggering over the last five years; the standard engine switched from the hybrid setup to the turbocharged inline-four and then back to the hybrid, for example. The biggest change, however, has been the addition of more fun variants: the off-road focused Tremor and the on-road oriented Lobo, the latter of which aims to Ouija-board the spirit of the original F-150 Lightning to the best of its front-wheel drive-based capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that but what if you already have a Maverick and want to add some zip? Or the Lobo’s just isn’t potent enough for you? Well, that’s where the new Maverick SV300T Package comes into play. But you’ll have to pony up Mustang-like money if you want to see your new compact pickup come equipped with it when you pick up your zero-mile new rig at the local Blue Oval dealer.

It has been revealed that the package—which, regrettably, shoves the numerical portion of its name between the letters to keep it from being a proper SVT—comes from the Ford Custom Garage, Dearborn’s in-house upgrade division, and ties together official Ford Racing parts and other Ford accessories to make a sportier Maverick. It’s made for AWD XLT, Lariat, and Lobo models, with the marquee attracting an engine reflash and a Mustang EcoBoost-sourced turbo and an upgraded intercooler to push power from 250 hp and 280 lb-ft to 300 hp and 250 lb-ft; there’s also a Borla exhaust. XLT and Lariat rigs gain Maverick Lobo shocks, lowering springs, and upgraded stabilizer components; they can also opt for an available front brake upgrade. (When we tested it earlier this year on a short autocross course, we found the effects of both power and exhaust both quite noticeable, while the upgraded suspension amped up the delights in the turns.).

On top of that, Ford throws in a few visual upgrades to help make the SV300T’s presence known even before people hear that Borla exhaust. 20-inch wheels come in either black or bronze, as do matching hood and body graphics. Specific lettering on the tailgate also comes along for the ride, and XLT and Lariat trim versions pick up a new lower front spoiler. Plus, if you buy the package with a new Maverick, performance-oriented tires are included, whereas customers adding it after purchase will have to pick them out separately.

Choosing to get the SV300T at purchase, however, means adding $13,395 to the price of a new Lobo, and $15,595 to an XLT or Lariat. Granted, that includes installation and allows owners to wrap it into the truck’s financing, but that still pushes the price to $49,680 for the XLT and $48,090 for the Lobo, based on 2027 model year pricing. (Ford’s announcement says it’s meant for 2025 and 2026 model year trucks, but considering it also mentions that the package is available on new Mavericks, it seems highly unlikely that it would not be available for 2027 ones too.).

Recent findings suggest that buy SV300T à la carte instead, and the pricing seems a bit more stomach-able; the XLT kit will run you $6075, and the Lobo version $4500. Keep in mind, though, doing so means you’ll have to have an ASE-certified tech handle the install, and you’ll still need to go out and buy fresh rubber on top of that to make the most of it.

According to recent reports, it has been decades since the move from coupe to convertible has come with serious compromise in rigidity or weight, so we're not expecting the Temerario Spyder to drop much in performance, but it's still reassuring to hear that the Temerario designers didn't just Sawzall the roof off and call it a day. The coupe’s aluminum spaceframe gets additional stiffening elements and reinforced mounting points, especially behind the seats where the folding roof sits when deployed. Lambo says it’s 6 percent stiffer in both static and dynamic torsional rigidity than the Huracan Spyder.

Lamborghini claims the Spyder will make a 0-to-62-mph run in 2.8 seconds, which is one tenth of a second behind its claim for the coupe. Top speed is a match at 213 mph. The Temerario Spyder comes on 20- or 21-inch wheels with a variety of Bridgestone sport, race, and even winter tires. The roof folds vertically, setting into position behind the seats along the spine of the car, which drops the center of gravity and leaves weight distribution basically unchanged, versus a horizontal stowage which would raise the center of gravity and move weight towards the rear wheels. This arrangement keeps the driving dynamics of the Temerario identical whether the roof is up or down.

When They Won’t (or Can’t) Connect: A Musician’s Notes on Listening

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • Industry observers note that A few days ago, I attended a talk at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs at the annual Yale Assembly for alumni delegates.
  • Sometimes it’s hard to know if people don’t want to connect, don’t know how, or both.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Industry observers note that A few days ago, I attended a talk at Yale’s Jackson School of Global Affairs at the annual Yale Assembly for alumni delegates. When I asked what the most pressing global problems are at the moment, the surprise that caught my ear was “the collapse of the recognition of facts.” When others cherry-pick data that serves their own agenda, it blocks connection. How well we respond to disconnection can have huge implications.

Sometimes it’s hard to know if people don’t want to connect, don’t know how, or both. At a class dinner out, the unexpected topic of parents came up. One parent seemed to find pleasure in music more than in her child. Another parent often said to his young daughter, who could not possibly read his adult mind, “You know what I mean, right?” Someone else repeatedly said, “You don’t know what it was like,” and yet could not answer his daughter’s questions about what his traumas were actually like.

Distinguishing “won’t connect” from “can’t connect” would help us understand the context of the disconnect, and that clarity helps us move forward.

According to recent reports, music is about connection, but musicians are not all naturally gifted at it. However, to stay afloat in the unsupported, wild west of the music industry, we have to upgrade our communication skills like everyone else. We have to connect with our audiences, supporters, partners, and presenters, even when the other side doesn’t want to – or doesn’t know how to – connect back.

Recent findings suggest that my work in music is often misunderstood to be the work of playing notes promptly and accurately. But it is the moment-to-moment listening and the consequent response that create the spirit of the piece, not the individual notes. This year I am taking my piano studio to perform in Rome, to practice performing as responding to a new environment in the moment.

Most of my time is spent listening for what is still missing. Building connections between the different musical elements helps me to infer the composer’s intent. In conversation too, creating a tensegrity of multidimensional motivations helps me to tease out what the speaker is not saying, before I make any interpretations.

In a recent development, author Iain McGilchrist posits that the search for truth requires four avenues of inquiry: science, reason, intuition, and imagination. We have to play with our awareness of not just the past and present, but the future. Only with whole-brain processing (both left and right sides) can we approach the complexity of truth.

Sources indicate that well-meaning people with a trust deficit may regress to hearing only their inner bubble of a few familiar themes and pre-formulated responses. We can challenge that response by labeling it, for example, “It seems like you are angry about this.” Even a wrong guess works, because they will have the urge to correct it, and that reveals something. If we are tolerant enough to wait and listen, we may draw out secrets that will change everything about our connection.

When we anticipate that a conversation or an encounter will not be pleasant, we greatly reduce its chances of building a connection. Our counterpart, when expecting friction, does the same.

Sources indicate that FBI negotiator Chris Voss shares a technique he calls “neutralizing negativity.” When we emotionally prepare the other side by saying “you are not going to like this,” you have taken the sting out of the interaction. I tried this with my Yale Alumni College class last week, where we studied two works by Mozart and Bartók. Before I introduced the difficult music of Bartók, I asked them to notice their posture towards their listening, as compared with how they had listened to the Mozart. While both works are intense, Mozart is associated with easy listening and Bartók with unpleasant dissonance. While listening to the unfamiliar dissonance of Bartók still took a lot of effort, the naming of this negative posture effectively helped people connect more than they would have otherwise.

It has been revealed that A colleague recently shared that when she volunteered to be a mentor, she discovered her mentees just wanted her contacts and did not want to connect. I don’t know whether to cry or laugh, because in my youth, I would have done anything to find mentors who wanted to connect with me and not just my success. I do still believe that with a persistent repetition of stating our values, we can build up both our integrity and their awareness for the potential of future connection. We have more power in calling out these moments than most of us realize or act on.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the above strategies worked for my business negotiations this week. But even if the connection had failed, I am still learning so much from processing these tricky relational crossroads. As Stephen Nachmanovitch writes in his marvelous book Free Play, “Trusting someone else can involve gigantic risks, and it leads to the even more challenging task of learning to trust yourself.” In music and in life, through the process of reaching out, we connect more deeply with ourselves.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that how do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells?
  • Industry observers note that unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, ford has entered the battery business. The first LFP battery cells are now rolling off the assembly line at Ford’s BlueOval Battery Park plant in Michigan and are headed to power Fathom prototypes in Kentucky.

Sources indicate that how do you get more out of a battery without adding weight or more cells? According to Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, who is also leading its Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, the answer lies in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology.

Industry observers note that unlike traditional lithium-ion, LFP batteries use no nickel or cobalt, which helps reduce costs. They also typically hold up better after years of use and charging.

According to recent reports, to make it a reality, Ford turned to CATL, the leading global EV battery manufacturer. Ford uses CATL’s licensed technology and manufacturing expertise at its BlueOval Battery Park Michigan plant.

Ford said it will be the first in the US to deliver LFP batteries for mainstream automotive use, with the battery cells now rolling off the line in Michigan.

The first LFP battery cells are headed to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant and will be used to power Fathom prototypes, its first vehicle based on the UEV platform.

Industry observers note that ford designed and engineered the Fathom from the ground up for efficiency. As such, it chose prismatic battery cells because they fit directly into the chassis, reducing structural costs.

With cells now being delivered from a plant that it owns and operates, Ford said it will use the knowledge gained in Michigan to support more affordable EVs and Ford Energy, its new battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

At Ford’s new battery plant in Michigan, assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it one of the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside China.

Recent findings suggest that “It's going to ruin my life,” he jokes to Men's Health in the paddock ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix. He's only managed to squeeze in about 25 minutes of gameplay so far this weekend, but his verdict is already in: “It's amazing.”.

Recent findings suggest that for now, at least, Hadjar has his priorities straight. “I'm a professional,” he notes with a smirk. “When I know it's time to go to sleep, I go to sleep.”.

That level of discipline extends well beyond bedtime. In a sport that demands lightning-fast reflexes, intense concentration, and serious physical endurance, Hadjar has developed a pretty specific routine to get his brain and body ready to perform.

In a recent development, take his pre-race ritual, which he has down to a science. He stretches and warms up with his trainer, including juggling and reaction-time tests to prime the brain. He listens to rap music—French, American, or British—to get himself hyped.

Then, exactly nine minutes before the race begins, he starts putting in his earpieces. “Not 10, not 11, nine," he claims.

It's not a superstition or a lucky number. (That would be six, the number he drives with for Red Bull.) It’s simply what he’s found to be the perfect amount of time to get in the car and get ready to race. “I hate staying in the car doing nothing,” he notes. “So for me, nine minutes is the maximum time.”.

While he enjoys the pre-race preparation, there's one part of training he'd happily skip: zone 2 cardio, running at a moderate pace to power up his endurance.

In a recent development, “It’s just boring. I like conditioning more,” he claims. To get through it, he puts on a movie, TV show, or music. “It goes by rapidly in the end, but it's just, I feel like it's a waste of time. But it's very crucial.”.

Recent findings suggest that when the race is over, Hadjar's routine is considerably more relaxed. A good meal helps him switch his brain off—specifically, a burger with caramelized onions, cheddar, tomato, and lettuce. He’ll also watch anime and FaceTime his parents, especially after a good result.

1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.
  • According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.
  • However, upcoming research published in the November 2026 concern of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, upcoming research published in the November 2026 concern of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

It has been revealed that A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

According to recent reports, researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

It has been revealed that among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, Newly introduced York, said these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”.

It has been revealed that banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more swiftly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s crucial for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she said.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

Recent findings suggest that “The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”.

According to recent reports, west Coast Customs has finished its first electric Chevy Bel Air, and there’s not much Chevy left under the paint. The Burbank shop cut the body off a Tesla Model 3, kept the entire rolling platform, and set a 1955 Bel Air shell on top of it.

In a recent development, the result, called Project B-Zero, looks like a ’55 Chevy from the curb and like a Model 3 as soon as you open the door. And it charges at Tesla Superchargers.

Recent findings suggest that in the shop’s fresh video, “The First Ever Electric Bel Air,” founder and CEO Ryan Friedlinghaus explains that a longtime client, Troy Swope, wants to convert an entire car collection to electric and picked the Bel Air to go first. WCC had previously built the same client a Chevelle with a big gas engine.

Friedlinghaus, who drives a Tesla himself, decided against pulling the Model 3’s motors and battery out and fitting them into the old Chevy. Instead, the Tesla stays whole and the Chevy becomes the body kit.

That’s a formula WCC has used for years with gas cars. The shop calls it “old school meets new school”: an old GTO body on a new GTO, an old Camaro on a new Camaro, an old Mustang on a new Mustang. B-Zero is the first time it did it with a Tesla underneath.

“It sounds easy, but that process was tedious,” Friedlinghaus noted.

Before any Chevy sheet metal went on, the crew took the bare Model 3 skateboard for a spin on the streets around the shop, with no doors, no lights and no seatbelts. Friedlinghaus joked about how many safety violations they were racking up. But it drove fine.

It has been revealed that the real headache was the wheelbase. A 1955 Chevy rides on a 115-inch wheelbase, while the Model 3 sits at 113.2 inches. On its gas builds, WCC can cut, shorten or lengthen the newer car’s frame to match the old body. You can’t do that with a Tesla, since the floor is the battery pack.

So the shop changed the body instead, stretching the Bel Air’s rear wheel wells so the wheels sit where they look like they belong.

The client wanted the exterior to read as a mostly stock Bel Air. The original car was red, so WCC kept it red, with a satin finish and gloss black accents.

Inside, it’s a Model 3. The shop kept the Tesla’s interior, including the steering wheel and center touchscreen, and modified it to fit the Chevy body. The seats got black suede with white stitching in an octagon pattern that Friedlinghaus mentioned was borrowed from the Lamborghini Urus, plus red accents and a “B-Zero” script on the dash.

Friedlinghaus noted the goal was for people to see “a really nice Bel Air” from the outside, then open the door and find a Tesla. He also expects some double takes when it pulls into a Supercharger station.

Industry observers note that he admits the reaction has been split. Plenty of people are mad that the shop electrified a Bel Air, and plenty of others think it came out great. The client is clearly in the second camp, describing the car as easy to drive and saying every trip in it feels like an event.

Here’s the full build video from West Coast Customs:.

This is sick. I know Tesla doesn’t care about personal car ownership anymore, but they should really sell their platform so shops can do these conversions without using salvage vehicles.

Recent findings suggest that well I was really interested in this build until I read how they kept it entirely Tesla inside. Not at all what I was thinking or what I'd call a true old car conversion to EV. Instead, they simply transformed the outside of a Tesla into an old looking car. To me, even the outside looks too far removed from the original Bel Air and more like a street rod. If that's what the owner wants and paid for, great.

Sources indicate that but for me, I would never do a conversion like that. I really want to convert an older 70's or 80's or early 90's Cadillac into an EV. But for me, I will insist that the outside and inside look 100% like the original car with just an EV powertrain.

Don’t get me wrong, if you can recycle a salvage, that’s good, but it can’t always be done.

Industry observers note that compare it to the 1966 Mustang that a Sacramento Tesla parts shop converted earlier this year. That project took about $40,000 and two years, with the team grafting sections of a Model 3 floor into the Mustang. It’s an amazing build, but it’s a lot of custom engineering. WCC’s approach skips most of that. You keep Tesla’s crash structure, battery thermal management, software, over-the-air updates and Supercharger access, because you never took the car apart in the first place. It’s closer to what S-Klub did with its Model 3-based Mercedes 300SL than a traditional drivetrain swap.

The purists will hate it. That’s fine. This Bel Air will get driven more in a year than most restored ones get driven in a decade.

WALKING IS A great way to keep a steady exercise routine, even when you're not in the mood for more intense workouts. Engaging in walking not only provides a gentle form of physical activity, but can also promote post-workout recovery and overall blood circulation. What can motivate you to get out for a few extra weekly walks? A pair of ultra-comfortable walking shoes that keep your feet happy long after you've reached your target.

Sources indicate that "All [walking] shoes should feel snug around your foot, have good arch support, the heel shouldn’t slip around, and there should be adequate room in the toe box," recommends Mark J. Mendeszoon, DPM, a board-certified podiatrist and foot and ankle surgeon.

In a recent development, since walking shoes can wear down quickly with everyday use, having one (or two) solid pairs in rotation is a smart move. Below, we’ve rounded up the best men’s walking shoes of the year—tested, podiatrist-reviewed, and chosen for comfort, support, and all-day wearability.

One crucial lesson we've learned from Mendeszoon is not to focus only on shoe length when determining your ideal fit. According to him, it's equally essential to consider shoe width—much like with running shoes. Many brands now offer a range of widths, so understanding your foot anatomy is key to the right fit. "Wear the same socks you wear when you walk when trying them on and remember that our feet expand while walking.".

Once you find the right pair, keep in mind to replace them after you've racked up some miles. "It is important to realize that shoes are generally good for 500 to 600 miles," indicates Mendeszoon. Even when you're primarily sporting them for walking. Ready to step into action? Then check out our guide to the best walking shoes for men below.

Its signature Smooth Metarocker geometry helps roll you forward with less effort, ideal for long walks, recovery days, or standing for hours. While it's technically a running shoe, walkers and all-day wearers have gravitated toward the Clifton for its smooth ride and day-to-night versatility.

In a recent development, I personally have had a lot of friends who love the Hoka Clifton 11 and are on their feet all day working in retail and hospitals. If you liked the 9 and 10, the 11 stays true to the formula—with subtle tweaks that make it feel just a little softer, a little smoother, and still seriously easy on the feet.

Recent findings suggest that look for walking shoes with support and stability features labeled for your specific foot type. "Consider your foot type and [walking] gait," states Dr. Bradley Schaeffer, DPM. "The goal is to keep your lower body in alignment as much as possible." Features such as a firm heel counter, a supportive midsole, and a secure lacing system can provide the stability you need for comfortable walking and to keep your feet properly aligned.

It has been revealed that when it comes to classification, if the shoe is stable, it is designed to help offset pronation, which is the inward rolling of the feet after landing on the ground. When a shoe is neutral, it lacks the stabilizing features, allowing your foot to fall more naturally. When a shoe is moderate, it is somewhere between those two worlds.

"Cushioning absorbs shock and helps to avoid tissue irritation and damage," explains Schaeffer. It's important to choose walking shoes with sufficient cushioning to absorb impact and shock with each step. Look for shoes with cushioned insoles and midsoles made from materials like foam or gel to ensure a comfortable walking experience, especially for longer walks or on hard surfaces.

In a recent development, decide if you prefer soft cushioning for impact absorption and comfort or a more responsive feel. Some shoes offer a balance between the two, so choose based on your preferences and walking style.

If you're in the market for a walking shoe to take you long distances frequently, be sure the models you're considering are relatively lightweight. Unless we're talking about a stability or trail shoe, which feature additional materials for added durability and support, that means under 11 ounces.

According to recent reports, pay attention to the upper material of the walking shoes, as it can impact comfort, breathability, and durability. Opt for shoes with breathable and flexible uppers made from materials like mesh or knit fabric to help keep your feet cool and comfortable. Additionally, keep an eye out for features like padded collars and tongues for even more comfort and support.

Recent findings suggest that I’m a certified strength and conditioning specialist based in Newly introduced York and a fitness writer who loves trying the latest gear and raving to my loved ones about his latest discoveries. I have a dog, and I take him for walks twice a day. I also trek through the city from Queens to Manhattan five to six times per week. I have a pretty full roster of clients that I see in-person for training sessions and hit about 15,000 to 20,000 steps per day. Needless to say, I am on my feet A LOT, so I need to be on top of my game when it comes to comfy footwear.

Industry observers note that I also got some assistance from Men’s Health fitness editors and medical advisors. We spent months of testing and researching to create this guide. Over the past few years, we’ve logged miles in more than 40 pairs of walking and running shoes from top brands like Asics, Hoka, Brooks, On, and more. Led by Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM and Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, along with expert input from podiatrists Schaeffer and Mendeszoon, we evaluated each shoe for fit, comfort, cushioning, support, durability, and value. We also considered real-world feedback from testers who wore these shoes during daily walks, commutes, and all-day wear.

From minimalist trainers to max-cushioned picks, we curated this list to meet a variety of foot types, walking styles, and comfort preferences—so you can find the pair that’s right for your stride.

Recent findings suggest that understanding your foot type is essential for finding the right walking shoes that offer optimal comfort and support. There are three primary arch types based on arch height: neutral, high, and flat. To determine your arch type, you can start with a simple "wet test," Mendeszoon recommends. Wet your feet and stand on a surface like concrete, sand, or a flattened paper bag. Examine the imprint left by your foot.

If your foot leaves a complete, flat imprint, you likely have low arches and would benefit from arch support or stability shoes. If the imprint shows the heel, outer side of the foot, ball of the foot, and toes, but not the arch, you might have a neutral or high arch.

In a recent development, while the wet test provides a basic idea, factors such as weight, biomechanics, and overall fitness also help determine your arch type accurately. For a more detailed analysis, consider visiting a local chiropractic clinic, podiatry practice, or high-quality running shoe store. Some locations offer foot scans that provide intricate information about your feet and arches.

It has been revealed that todd Sinett from Tru Whole Care in New York highlights a special machine called the Foot Levelers Digital Foot Scanner, which identifies specific pressure points on your feet that could be linked to back pain. This advanced tool offers precise measurements for customized orthotics, ensuring tailored support for your unique foot structure.

Sources indicate that yes, running shoes can absolutely be worn for walking, according to Mendeszoon. In fact, they may offer some added benefit compared to conventional walking shoes.

According to recent reports, running shoes are designed to absorb the impact of running, which means they can also provide good shock absorption when walking. Many people choose to wear running shoes for walking because of added support and flexibility, too.

In a recent development, one downside: Running shoes tend to be heavier and less breathable than walking shoes because of their more durable design. So, it's important to note that they may not be the best choice for long-distance walking.

It's important to replace your walking shoes regularly to ensure adequate support and cushioning, probably more frequently than you think. As a general rule of thumb, it's recommended to replace walking shoes every 300 to 500 miles (or every 3 to 5 months for those who walk for at least 45 minutes at least 3 times per week).

The specific lifespan of a shoe depends on several factors, including the frequency and intensity of use, the shoe's quality, and the type of surface you typically walk on. There are a few signs to look out for that may indicate it's time to replace your shoes:.

It has been revealed that ultimately, it's key to listen to your body and pay attention to any signs of discomfort or pain when walking. If you notice any of the above signs, it's a good idea to start looking for a latest pair of walking shoes.

Powerlifting legend Mark Bell is a huge fan of walking for weight loss, as is Will Smith. This guy lost 60 pounds with walking and bodyweight workouts. And this guy lost 200 pounds by walking and eating a CICO diet. It's all about starting to add to your daily step count, and really sticking with it.

"Starting slow and working your way up is better than overdoing it and giving up," Chris Gagliardi, a certified personal trainer at the American Council on Exercise, previously told Men's Health. An easy way to approach it: Commit to a quick 10-minute walk after dinner, and gradually increase the duration as you become more comfortable with daily movement.

Step counting also helps. "If you’re only getting 3,000 steps on a typical day, don’t try to get 10,000 steps the next day. That can be really discouraging. Aim for 5,000 every day for a week. Then go up to 7,000 the next week," walking coach Michele Stanten, founder of MyWalkingCoach.com and author of The Walking Solution, previously told Men's Health.

He  still enjoys working out, running  and coaching runners of all ages.

Breaking: The Music of Thanksgiving: Thirty Voices at One Table

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.
  • In a recent development, thanksgiving as a musical holiday?
  • Christmas has its carols and the Fourth of July its rousing bands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

In a recent development, thanksgiving as a musical holiday? What possibilities!

Christmas has its carols and the Fourth of July its rousing bands. Thanksgiving is usually defined by motion and aroma, the joyful hum of conversation, the clatter of silverware (or plasticware), the scent of favorite holiday family foods, perhaps the sound of bickering siblings (both young and adult), and the sigh of aahs when the turkey finally emerges from the oven.

This year our gathering will have a new sound: two grandmothers leading the family in song.

Sources indicate that we’re bringing together two extended families, about thirty people under one roof. The youngest is three years old; the oldest is seventy-six. Many ages, memories, opinions, football fans, and personalities are all under one roof. After dinner, or perhaps before everyone hits the food sleepies, we’ll sing “Over the River and Through the Wood,” followed by “You Are My Sunshine.”.

It has been revealed that some will know every word. Others may remember only the chorus. The youngest may sing a few words, hum, add their own sounds, or even bang out the beat with a wooden spoon. What fun as the elders turn down their hearing aids. Someone may come in early; someone else may be a beat behind. And of course, good old Uncle, who we won’t name, can’t carry a tune. This is not a choir that has rehearsed together, although Ethan and Sara will help guide us. We’re gathering as a family, not auditioning for a TV talent show.

The two songs we chose to begin carry different kinds of familiarity. “Over the River and Through the Wood” belongs to the season, with its image of traveling to a family gathering. “You Are My Sunshine” is a song many people have known since childhood, although the version one person remembers may not be quite the version another learned. We may have to help each other with a word or two, and someone may remember a verse the rest of us have forgotten.

The song sheet is a simple idea, but we like the question at the bottom. “What else should we sing?” might bring up a song someone’s parent used to sing, a tune from a school play, or something the children are listening to now. A suggestion may come with a story the family has heard many times before, but still loves to hear. Sometimes a song is a favorite because it’s funny, easy to sing, or simply familiar.

Sources indicate that the toddler might not know all the words, and the teenagers might roll their eyes before joining in, increasing the volume of the room. Someone might begin to think about doing the dishes, but for a few brief moments, we might have the gift of nobody checking a phone — just the collective shared wave of sound and rhythm.

Singing together can help coordinate our breathing and even influence patterns in our heart rates. But you don't need to measure any of that to notice what happens when people sing together. We listen to one another, adjust our voices, and try to stay with the group.

A large family gathering doesn’t often ask everyone to do the same thing at once. In smaller Thanksgiving gatherings, we’ve gone around the table asking questions like, “What are you grateful for" and "What have you done to help someone else feel grateful?" We use a homemade placemat asking about gratitude.

People catch up in small groups. The children move in and out of the room. Someone is tending to the food while someone else clears a place at the table. Singing gives us a few minutes with one shared activity.

Hopefully, a song sheet encourages all voices and squeals to join in. Inviting family members to suggest a favorite tune shifts the dynamic to active participation and gives everyone a voice. When you ask people what they want to sing, you are really asking: What memory do you bring to this table? What tune makes you feel at home?

According to recent reports, the songs aren’t performance, just connection. We know that someone may have to retrieve a wandering toddler or may pause while a plate is passed or a child asks for something from the kitchen. The music may stop and start. In a gathering of thirty people, a perfectly uninterrupted performance seems unlikely.

Afterward, we’ll return to the conversations already underway, half of us forgetting what we were talking about anyway. People will share dessert, tell stories, and catch up with relatives they don’t see every week. Later, when the house is quieter, there may be time for a longer conversation or a cup of coffee. Those parts of the day matter, too.

In a recent development, gratitude is often a quiet reflection, perhaps first thing in the morning, or quietly before falling asleep. Thanksgiving is a social ritual, giving us the chance to make our gratitude visible and communal.

Long before the final slice of pie is served, a shared song reminds us why we gathered in the first place. Sure, we'll also eat too much, complain about how stuffed we are, and probably fall asleep earlier than planned.

As the holiday draws to a close and the house settles down, the music we made may linger in memory. Maybe during the car rides home, someone hums “You Are My Sunshine.”.

When the final chord fades, what remains is the warmth of the ensemble, how it made us feel, collectively, and tunes we will hold on to for next year.

Rivian’s newly introduced electric bike spinoff, ALSO, has hit another speed bump. The organization has revealed that it is temporarily halting deliveries of its TM-B electric bicycles after discovering software-related problems affecting some bikes, including challenges with charging behavior.

And unfortunately, this isn’t entirely surprising. We’ve already reported on some strange battery behavior with the newly introduced e-bikes, as well as customers having to send their bikes back for repairs.

In a message sent to customers, ALSO explained that it was pausing shipments to address several software problems before more bikes reach riders.

“We’ve identified a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior, that are impacting some bikes,” the organization explained.

ALSO claims its engineers are working on a firmware enhancement to resolve the problems, with shipments expected to resume in approximately two weeks.

The pause affects the remaining Launch Edition deliveries as well as the beginning of Performance Edition shipments, both of which will now arrive later than previously promised.

The announcement follows earlier reports of unusual charging and discharging behavior on the TM-B, which we previously highlighted as some of the growing pains facing Rivian’s ambitious new e-bike venture.

We’ve also reported on customers needing to return their bikes for repairs, raising questions about how smoothly the organization’s initial rollout was progressing.

The issues align with many of our initial concerns we discussed a year ago when the bike was first unveiled, namely that the high-tech design means the bike incorporates many latest and proprietary systems that could each lead to complicated and costly failures.

Now ALSO has officially acknowledged software problems affecting some bikes, including charging behavior, though it hasn’t detailed the full extent of the concerns or confirmed whether they are directly related to those earlier reports.

I love the PR spin how only "some" bikes are affected. If it's the same bike running the same software, it's affected. The only bikes not affected are the ones that haven't been delivered, because they are not being used.

The bike represents a fairly radical departure from traditional electric bicycles, with proprietary technology throughout its drivetrain and control systems. That makes software an especially important part of the ownership experience.

In a recent development, to ALSO’s credit, pausing deliveries to fix known problems is probably the right move. Nobody wants to receive a premium-priced electric bicycle only to discover that it needs an immediate trip back to the manufacturer.

But for customers who have already waited longer than expected, another delay is undoubtedly frustrating.

ALSO says it will provide another revision on November 24, hopefully with better news about when deliveries can resume.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Machina’s business is based around its RoboCraftsman platform, which it basically pitches as a factory in a box.
  • According to recent reports, machina Labs was founded in 2019 and so far has mostly served clients in the aerospace and defense industries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Automotive manufacturing is a laborious, resource-intensive process. While the complex metropolises that are modern car factories work well for high-volume products, it is often prohibitively expensive for automakers to retool these plants to create distinct body panels for limited-production models. Now a California-based company called Machina Labs aims to plug that gap with an innovative metal manufacturing process that promises speed, flexibility, and cost-savings.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07036.

Machina’s business is based around its RoboCraftsman platform, which it basically pitches as a factory in a box. The system uses a pair of large robotic arms to perform a variety of tasks on metal panels, from striking designs into pre-stamped panels to fully forming new pieces. The robotic arms are controlled by software that can switch between different projects as promptly as Machina can upload new designs, and the system also scans the completed panel to see if any additional work needs to be done, and to trim, finish, and heat treat the pieces. The entire setup can be folded into two shipping containers that can then be easily transported.

According to recent reports, machina Labs was founded in 2019 and so far has mostly served clients in the aerospace and defense industries. But now Machina wants to enter the automotive space, launching a new division called Machina Rebellis. With its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina aims to give automakers a way to skip the costly retooling process, with its technology providing a more efficient method to rapidly craft customizable body panels, allowing OEMs to efficiently build more distinctive limited-edition cars.

According to recent reports, machina’s interest in the automotive world started a few years back when it built a truck called the Anvil, based on the Ford F-150 Lightning, to demonstrate the unique body panels its metalworking machines could produce. While still fairly crude, this early prototype got Toyota’s attention, and the Japanese automotive giant is now an investor in Machina Labs via Woven Capital, Toyota’s venture capital division.

The process has improved vastly since the Anvil was built, and to demonstrate this, Machina Labs created a new show vehicle, the Lassen, which is being shown at the Los Angeles auto show. Based on a Toyota Tacoma, the Lassen wears a unique hood, tailgate, and fenders, showing off the sort of customization that Machina’s process is capable of. Machina worked with Callum, the design house formed by Ian Callum, to pen the look of these panels before manufacturing them using the RoboCraftsman platform.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07036.

It has been revealed that while the Lassen isn’t a drastic departure from a standard Tacoma, the changes that Machina made would typically take around four to six months to produce via traditional methods, the company stated at a media event at its second factory in Chatsworth, California. Using its RoboCraftsman platform, Machina was able to take the Lassen from sketches to a finished product in just two and a half weeks.

The Lassen shows off Machina’s two main capabilities. The hood and tailgate demonstrate the RoboCraftsman’s ability to re-strike pre-stamped panels with custom designs. The Lassen’s tailgate has a bold embossed Machina script, while the hood also notes Machina and has a topographical map of its namesake, Mount Lassen in California. The RoboCraftsman platform can put just about any design on a metal panel, and Machina also had tailgates on display featuring a retro Toyota design and a Los Angeles Rams logo.

The fenders, meanwhile, are entirely newly introduced panels formed by the RoboCraftsman, and they have a bulging, powerful look. These fenders started as a sheet of metal—Machina works in both aluminum and steel—before being shaped by the robotic arms. This process is a bit slower than the re-striking process, which can take minutes to complete, but a fully formed panel can be finished within hours.

Sources indicate that machina believes its RoboCraftsman platform is best suited to production runs in the hundreds and thousands. This could include special-edition models for large OEMs, or working with aftermarket companies to create body kits and other visual customizations. OEMs can also use Machina’s process to promptly create body panels for early pre-production vehicles, typically an expensive and time-consuming part of the development cycle. In the future, Machina also envisions sending its RoboCraftsman units directly to OEM manufacturing sites to speed up the process even further.

Over the past decade, high-end carmakers realized there is a lot of money in personalization, leading to a surge of one-off and limited-production supercars, designed to the exacting specification desired by their wealthy buyers. These cars, often hand-built, are incredibly expensive. Machina Labs states that its RoboCraftsman platform could democratize customization, with the speed and flexibility at which it can work allowing automakers to save money and offer personalized details on more ordinary, everyday vehicles.

The RoboCraftsman platform provides a way to rapidly manufacture custom body panels, and the flexibility to switch among a large number of different projects in a short amount of time. The Lassen serves as a proof of concept as Machina courts automotive companies, and seeing the RoboCraftsman operate in person, we certainly see a space in the automotive world for Machina’s quick and flexible manufacturing innovation.

If your domicile happens to exist, say, under a large boulder, you might not have heard that Grand Theft Auto VI is finally arriving at the stroke of midnight on November 19. Those of us who watch television, browse the web, scroll social media, listen to the radio, read the newspaper, flip through magazines, or consume outside info in any way are well aware of the video game, however. It’s the latest installment of the immensely popular “Grand Theft Auto” series, which combines a (surprisingly deep) vein of car culture with an immersive open world full of theft, fighting, drugs, and other violent delights.

While the previous games came out on a semi-regular schedule of one every few years, it’s been 13 trips ‘round the sun since the last one hit stores. (GTA VI’s development has been so delayed, it even inspired a meme.) Suffice it to say, there’s a lot of pent-up anticipation—even enough to spark half-founded panic headlines about millions of people around the world call in sick to play. But there’s another report that puts a bit more solid of a figure on the excitement around the game. According to digital analysis firm SensorTower, GTA VI has already racked up $1.65 billion in pre-sales ahead of its launch.

That correlates to a little over 17 million orders for the game so far, according to the report, with 75 percent of pre-sales going for the PlayStation 5 version and the other 25 percent for Xbox Series X|S consoles. The chart shows a fairly typical exponential curve growth over the last five months since pre-sales kicked off: a long period of incremental gains, followed by rapid acceleration in the last few weeks.

And GTA VI-based revenue seems likely to keep coming in to creator Rockstar Games’s coffers at quite a clip, considering initial reviews for the game have been stellar so far. While it may not be your typical automotive-themed driving game, the latest release seems all but sure to guarantee Grand Theft Auto remains a serious part of car culture for some time to come.
